reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
clinicalPearls: An accessory navicular is a common accessory ossicle on the medial side of the navicular, present in a significant minority of feet and usually asymptomatic
Symptoms arise when the ossicle becomes painful at the insertion of the tibialis posterior tendon, producing medial midfoot pain and a tender bony prominence

The type II accessory navicular, joined to the navicular by a cartilaginous synchondrosis into which the tibialis posterior inserts, is the type most likely to become symptomatic through shear across that junction
Pain is aggravated by activity and by footwear pressing on the medial prominence, and there may be an associated flatfoot
Because the tibialis posterior inserts onto the ossicle, symptomatic cases can be associated with tibialis posterior dysfunction and a flexible flatfoot deformity
Weight-bearing radiographs including an external oblique view demonstrate the ossicle and its type, while MRI shows oedema across the synchondrosis in symptomatic cases
Distinguish it from tibialis posterior tendinopathy, navicular stress fracture, and midfoot arthritis

Initial management is conservative with supportive orthoses and medial arch support, footwear modification, activity modification, and physiotherapy, with excision of the ossicle and tibialis posterior reconstruction reserved for resistant cases
reference.pathophysiology: The accessory navicular is a secondary ossification centre on the medial aspect of the navicular that fails to fuse, and it is intimately related to the insertion of the tibialis posterior tendon. In the commonly symptomatic type II variant, the ossicle is connected to the navicular by a fibrocartilaginous synchondrosis, and much of the tibialis posterior inserts onto the ossicle rather than directly onto the navicular. Repetitive traction and shear from the tibialis posterior across this synchondrosis, together with direct pressure from footwear on the bony prominence, produce pain, local inflammation, and stress across the junction, which MRI shows as oedema. Because the tibialis posterior is the principal dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch, an insertion compromised by a symptomatic accessory navicular can be associated with tibialis posterior dysfunction and a flexible flatfoot. Acute exacerbations may follow minor trauma or a twisting injury that stresses the synchondrosis.
additionalDifferentials: Medial midfoot ganglion or soft-tissue lesion
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing foot radiographs including an external oblique view to identify the ossicle and its type
Clinical examination for a tender medial prominence and assessment of tibialis posterior function and arch
MRI to demonstrate oedema across the synchondrosis and assess the tibialis posterior tendon
Single-limb heel-raise and too-many-toes assessment where flatfoot coexists
Ultrasound to evaluate the tibialis posterior tendon insertion where indicated
Comparison views of the contralateral foot given the frequent bilaterality
Bone scan in selected cases to confirm the ossicle as the pain source
redFlags: A painful, progressive flatfoot suggesting associated tibialis posterior rupture or dysfunction
Focal navicular tenderness with activity-related pain suggesting a navicular stress fracture
A rigid, painful flatfoot suggesting tarsal coalition rather than a simple accessory navicular
Signs of infection or a destructive lesion at the medial midfoot
reference.prognosis: Most symptomatic accessory naviculars settle with conservative measures aimed at offloading the tibialis posterior insertion and supporting the arch, particularly in adolescents whose symptoms often improve with skeletal maturity. When symptoms persist, excision of the ossicle with reattachment or reconstruction of the tibialis posterior gives good pain relief in the majority, although recovery is gradual and associated flatfoot may need to be addressed.
pitfalls: Dismissing medial midfoot pain as simple tendinopathy and missing a symptomatic accessory navicular
Failing to recognise associated tibialis posterior dysfunction and flatfoot
Overlooking a navicular stress fracture presenting with similar medial pain
Excising the ossicle without securing the tibialis posterior insertion, weakening arch support
Not considering tarsal coalition when the flatfoot is rigid
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
management: Initial conservative management with activity modification, relative rest and simple analgesia or NSAIDs for pain
Offload the tibialis posterior insertion and support the medial longitudinal arch with orthoses and supportive footwear that avoids pressure over the bony prominence
A short period of immobilisation in a walking boot or cast for acute or refractory symptoms
Physiotherapy with tibialis posterior strengthening and stretching once acute pain settles, particularly where a flexible flatfoot coexists
Consider a corticosteroid injection around the synchondrosis in selected refractory cases
Surgical excision of the ossicle with reattachment or advancement of the tibialis posterior tendon (Kidner-type procedure) for symptoms failing conservative care
Reassure adolescents that symptoms often improve with skeletal maturity
